We are not authorized to publish PRoot sources yet. This website is currently a preview. Thanks your feedback anyway :)

I keep this issue open until the official public release.

For the record, here is how to reproduce the problem:

```
    host$ proot -Q 'qemu-arm -g 1234' /path/to/arm/rootfs
    # waiting for GDB client ... connected

    guest$ /usr/bin/echo "Hello world"
    bind: Address already in use
    qemu: could not open gdbserver on port 1234
```

The following solution works with QEMU 1.0 and later only.  First, ask
to each instance of QEMU to unset the QEMU_GDB environment variable:

```
    proot -Q 'qemu-arm -U QEMU_GDB' ...
```

Then, set this variable to the expected port number right before
executing the program you want to debug.  For examples:
- to debug the first process (parent):

```
    env QEMU_GDB=1234 proot -Q 'qemu-arm -U QEMU_GDB' ...
    # waiting for GDB client
```
- to debug a process launched interactively (or in a script):

```
    host$ proot -Q 'qemu-arm -U QEMU_GDB' ...

    guest$ /usr/bin/echo "Hello world"
    Hello world

    guest$ env QEMU_GDB=1234 /usr/bin/echo "Hello world"
    # waiting for GDB client
```
- to debug a child process: add a call to `setenv()` before the call
  to `exec()`.  It's a bit intrusive in this case but it's a reliable
  solution.

It works because QEMU 1.0+ handles options passed through environment
variable before command-line options, thus QEMU_GDB is unset after
being used by QEMU itself.  Finally, only the first QEMU instance that
sees this variable is affected.  Note that it works with any QEMU
options (see `qemu-arm -h`).

The following error is due to another problem in PRoot v2.0 when using QEMU v1.1:

```
Registering `cpu' which already exists
```

I'm investigating.

Actually, the problem is reproducible without PRoot:

```
/lib64/ld-linux-x86-64.so.2 arm-linux-user/qemu-arm
Registering `arm-cpu' which already exists
Aborted
```

We just have to ask PRoot to not use the dynamic linker as a loader:

```
env PROOT_IGNORE_ELF_INTERPRETER=1 proot -q qemu-arm ./rootfs/
```

I will submit a patch for PRoot today.

Please, could you confirm PRoot v2.0.1 solves these problems?

> proot -Q qemu-arm ./media/rootfs/
> proot warning: can't create the guest path (binding) "/proc/self/mounts": you can still access it _directly_, without seeing it though

I got this. Is it normal?
Well, this is not unexpected.  I could confirm that only if you specify what the guest and host distros are.
Both are archlinux.

In your guest rootfs, "/etc/mtab" points to "/proc/self/mounts" but PRoot fails at creating "/proc/self". However this shouldn't create any trouble.

For information, these kind of warnings will disappear in the next release of PRoot (thanks to a new feature).

To complete the report, when I leave a single binding, even if there is no error, actually two consecutive runs of proot do not behave the same way:
- with the /opt/gcc-build:/work1/gcc-build binding, starting with no /rootfs/opt dir
- the first time, after the execution, the /rootfs/opt dir is created but empty
- running a second time, the /rootfs/opt/gcc-build dir is now created.

I would expect that at the first run proot creates the /rootfs/opt/gcc-build dir.
Thanks for this report. It is now fixed in the new version of PRoot (v2.3)

You're right, it's related to $ORIGIN in rpath.

Technically, the problem is exposed by PRoot because it uses the ELF
interpreter as a loader.  It is reproducible without PRoot this way:
- /lib64/ld-linux-x86-64.so.2 path/to/java => works
- /lib64/ld-linux-x86-64.so.2 link/to/java => doesn't work

At a first glance, the ELF interpreter gets the actual path to the
executable through /proc/self/exe.  Sadly, when used as a loader, it
doesn't check /proc/self/exe at all.  This is not the only issue
encountered when the ELF interpreter is used as a loader [1](https://groups.google.com/d/msg/proot_me/pbkgC-a66n4/FVs2URo6atAJ), that's
why PRoot should move to a custom ELF loader this year.  I keep this
issue open until then.

Great to hear that you tracked down the issue, and that there's a fix on the way at some point. For the moment, it's relatively easy to work around by just adding the java bin directory to $PATH in the PRoot.

Thanks again for looking into this, and thanks a ton for this awesome utility!

Hello @jonbrett, thanks for the bug report!

Sadly, seccomp-filter is broken on Ubuntu 13.04: https://bugs.launchpad.net/ubuntu/+source/linux/+bug/1202161

I'll patch PRoot soon to disable seccomp-filter when `execve` fails because of such a kernel bug.  In the mean time, you can use the workaround suggested by @aejsmith (PROOT_NO_SECCOMP).

Regards,
Cedric.

I confirm seccomp-filter works fine with **vanilla** 3.8 kernels, and it _seems_ to be fixed on Ubuntu 13.10: https://bugs.launchpad.net/ubuntu/+source/linux/+bug/1202161/comments/6  As of today, I have no idea how they broke this feature :(

The busybox .config is from OpenWrt r36941, with a dynamic loader from
uClibc patched to enable standalone binary execution in its config. The
patch is in ldinst.txt which is downloadable at
https://sites.google.com/site/taldewandroid/get. This was on a Samsung
Replenish android phone, using the OpenWrt at91 platform rootfs.tar.gz
binaries (see http://downloads.openwrt.org/ ). The relevant code  is at
https://sites.google.com/site/taldewandroid/get.

As an aside: I have also encountered errors with the OpenWrt rootfs in the
numbers in programs; e.g. vim will say that there are some gigantic amount
of lines, busybox ls will give wrong file sizes. Other tested rootfs's have
been OK; so the problem is likely in one or some of these: openwrt at91
rootfs/binaries; the device itself; the kernel/userspace on the device.

Thanks for your assistance!

PRoot really replaces brk(2) with mmap(2) during "sysenter" (and swap them back during "sysexit") [1] to avoid an actual bug in Bash when loaded with a user-mode ELF loader.  This bug can be reproduced _without_ PRoot by executing this script [2] several times (if ASLR is enabled).

I let this issue open if you have more questions or comments.

Cédric.

This is exactly the Bash bug PRoot heap emulation [1] attempts to
workaround.  Sadly, in your case, the pre-allocated heap size is not
big enough.

Rant: why the heck Bash developers assume the heap has an
infinite size?  Googling confirms this causes troubles even without an
ELF loader.

I let this issue open until I find a reliable solution (maybe using a
custom ELF loader).  In the mean time, you can try to increase the
pre-allocated heap size [2].

> Perhaps using MREMAP_MAYMOVE with mremap(2) could help ?

It is not possible to move the [emulated] heap since the application
might have variables that point inside it, and PRoot doesn't redirect
memory accesses (it is way too costly).

Cédric.

For the record, I talked with Carlos off-line.  Here are the minutes:
- this issue happens when executing STWorkbench;
- on Fedora 17 32-bit (not 64-bit); and
- it depends on the installation of the JVM (to be confirmed)

@cprada, you can reproduce this issue _without_ PRoot using the virtual machine you provided me:

```
$ setarch $(uname -m) -R  env LD_LIBRARY_PATH=/usr/lib/jvm/java-1.7.0-openjdk-1.7.0.25/jre/lib/i386/client:/usr/lib/jvm/java-1.7.0-openjdk-1.7.0.25/jre/lib/i386 /lib/ld-linux.so.2 /opt/STM/STWorkbench-R6.4.0/stworkbench/STWorkbench
Error occurred during initialization of VM
Could not reserve enough space for object heap
```

Curiously enough, it doesn't happen when changing slightly the LD_LIBRARY_PATH environment variable (adding a redundant '/' in front of the first absolute path):

```
$ setarch $(uname -m) -R  env LD_LIBRARY_PATH=//usr/lib/jvm/java-1.7.0-openjdk-1.7.0.25/jre/lib/i386/client:/usr/lib/jvm/java-1.7.0-openjdk-1.7.0.25/jre/lib/i386 /lib/ld-linux.so.2 /opt/STM/STWorkbench-R6.4.0/stworkbench/STWorkbench
<it works>
```

As of my understanding, PRoot (and "setarch + ld-linux.so.2") slightly changes the memory layout and this makes STWorkbench/JVM fail to allocate [more than] 1GB of continuous memory.  This exposes that STWorkbench/JVM is very close to the address space layout limit on 32-bit Linux systems (3GB).

Cédric.

Currently PRoot relies on the ELF interpreter ("/lib/ld-uClibc.so.0" in your case) to load programs, as a  consequence this feature must be explicitly enabled in uClibC configuration: LDSO_STANDALONE_SUPPORT=y (this is not the case in the rootfs you provided).

In the future, PRoot will have its own ELF loader so it will be more transparent to users.

Hello @fluxer,

By default, PRoot changes the [guest] current working directory
to $PWD (ie. same as the host one).  This is useful when
launching programs in the guest rootfs using a relative
path ("./configure" is a typical example).  Of course this
assumes that $PWD is bound/mounted into the the guest rootfs,
hence the following warning when it's not the case:

```
proot warning: can't chdir("[...]") in the guest rootfs: No such file or directory
proot info: default working directory is now "/"
```

Regarding the -R option, it is similar to the -r option but it
also binds/mounts a couple of "useful" directories into the guest
rootfs.  In your example, one of this "useful" directory ($HOME)
is a parent of $PWD:

```
$ pwd
/home/smil3y/Desktop/builder
```

As a consequence, the "chdir($PWD)" performed by PRoot into the
guest rootfs succeed.  This is expected (remember
the "./configure" example).

Now if you move to -- let's say -- "/etc" before running PRoot,
you'll be in the "/etc" directory from the guest rootfs (I agree
that could be confusing):

```
$ cd /etc
$ cat slackware-version 
Slackware 14.1

$ proot -R ~/rootfs/gentoo-amd64-hardened+nomultilib/
$ cat slackware-version 
/bin/cat: slackware-version: No such file or directory

$ cat gentoo-release 
Gentoo Base System release 2.2
```

Another example, if you move to a directory that exists into the
host rootfs but that doesn't exist into the guest rootfs, you'll
get the expected warning:

```
$ cd /usr/x86_64-slackware-linux/
$ proot -R ~/rootfs/gentoo-amd64-hardened+nomultilib/
proot warning: can't chdir("/usr/x86_64-slackware-linux/./.") in the guest rootfs: No such file or directory
proot info: default working directory is now "/"
```

If you don't want your $HOME bound/mounted into the guest rootfs,
either use the -r option with explicit -b options:

```
$ proot -r guest-rootfs/      \
        -b /etc/host.conf     \
        -b /etc/hosts         \
        -b /etc/hosts.equiv   \
        -b /etc/mtab          \
        -b /etc/netgroup      \
        -b /etc/networks      \
        -b /etc/passwd        \
        -b /etc/group         \
        -b /etc/nsswitch.conf \
        -b /etc/resolv.conf   \
        -b /etc/localtime     \
        -b /dev/              \
        -b /sys/              \
        -b /proc/             \
```

or use the -R option, then (order matters) bound/mount an empty
directory over $HOME:

```
$ mkdir empty
$ proot -R guest-rootfs -b empty:/home/smil3y/
```

Please, let me know if you think we can make this default
behavior less confusing.

Regards,
Cédric.

Hi there,
You could achieve this with an extension that acts in 2 steps:
1. Intercept the _chroot_ system call through the _SYSCALL_ENTER_END_ event in order to remember the argument given to _chroot_, and also disable the system call itself because you want to spoof it and not let it return an error.
2. Change and check all paths through the _GUEST_PATH_ and _HOST_PATH_ events (see [here](https://github.com/proot-me/PRoot/blob/master/src/extension/extension.h) for what they mean). With these you can append the chroot argument and verify if it holds or is invalid.

The only issue I see here is with detecting when the _chroot_ jail is stopped. Maybe by detecting when _Ctrl + C_ or _exit_ are typed in. If you have control over the program that uses PRoot, you could spark a certain event yourself that it could use as a stop command.

The chroot jail is stopped when chroot is called on a relative directory (usually one opened and saved before chroot) and the chroot is set to another alternative absolute path -- usually /

I came across a similar problem with Python3.5 this time.

## TL;DR

I've got an explanation, a workaround, and the TL;DR is: not sure something could be improved in the way CARE works: it's more to do with how Python works so Python users => ~~switch to a better language~~ / be careful :trollface: 

## Full description

Here we go for the whole picture.

A minimal working example to reproduce this would be:

```
# skip output for the first 2 commands
➜ care -r ~ -o /tmp/python3_basic.tgz.bin python3 -c 'print("hello")'
➜ /tmp/python3_basic.tgz.bin

# successful re-execution
➜  /tmp /tmp/python3_basic/re-execute.sh 
hello

# failed re-execution
➜  /tmp /tmp/python3_basic/re-execute.sh > /tmp/foo  
Fatal Python error: Py_Initialize: can't initialize sys standard streams
AttributeError: module '_bootlocale' has no attribute 'getpreferredencoding'

Current thread 0x00007f7c737bb700 (most recent call first):
proot info: pid 10109: terminated with signal 6
```

The problem occurs when Python initialises, it loads a sequence of default packages (you can see them using the `-v` flag on the command line).

As for any other python package, the interpreter (at least CPython) looks first for a previously “compiled” version of the package (the .pyc) and loads it instead of the equivalent .py if it finds any.

_Quoting @ghisvail_

> Whatever module you import (not the executed script),
> the byte code executed by the Python VM will be cached in these .pyc
> files.
> 
> With Python 2, they can be found alongside the corresponding .py files.
> With Python 3, they are stored in a separate __pycache__ folder in the
> folder where the module is located.
> 
> 

The problem of this loading sequence with CARE / Proot is that if the .pyc contains some platform dependent data (it seems to be something with the encoding here), the only the .pyc is captured in the archive. The .py is present but empty, I assume because it wasn’t read.

```
# file's size is 0!!
➜  /tmp find python3_basic/rootfs -name '_bootlocale.py' -exec ls -lh {} \; 
-rw-r--r-- 1 jopasserat users 0 Jan  3 04:40 python3_basic/rootfs/usr/lib/python3.5/_bootlocale.py
```

_Quoting @ghisvail again_

> 
> The cache files contain platform dependent data. I
> believe you can instruct the Python interpreter to not save these cache
> files via an environment variable (PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE), or
> invoking the interpreter with the -B flag.

There's also something I couldn't clearly understand but this problem occurs only when the stdout/err of the Python interpreter are redirected / or captured by another program than the running shell. This is what happens when calling the `re-execute.sh` script from another application or simply by redirecting its output with bash's `>`

## Conclusion 

I'm closing this issue as it doesn't seem related to CARE itself but very specific to some Python intrinsic. More than happy to re-open if someone with more Python-fu knows how to circumvent this from happening when archiving.

Until then, careful pythonists!

Hi,
This extension works by intercepting the _bind_ and _listen_ syscalls,
but I've seen that _socketcall_ is used instead in some architectures.
Especially in a very important one, which is x86-32 (for kernels below 4.3).

As stated by the _socketcall_'s man page:

>  On a some architectures—for example, x86-64 and ARM—there is no
       socketcall() system call; instead socket(2), accept(2), bind(2), and
       so on really are implemented as separate system calls. 
> On x86-32, socketcall() was historically the only entry point for the
       sockets API.  However, starting in Linux 4.3, direct system calls are
       provided on x86-32 for the sockets API.  This facilitates the
       creation of seccomp(2) filters that filter sockets system calls (for
       new user-space binaries that are compiled to use the new entry
       points) and also provides a (very) small performance improvement.

So one remaining thing for this extension to work on x86 32bits systems 
is to intercept _socketcall_ and redirect to the bind/connect translation functions.

Hi there,
The `read-only` feature isn't natively included in PRoot,
though there are solutions that might approach what you want:
- Creating the `read-only` symlink beforehand, that will act as a `read-only` filter, and then bind it with PRoot. Though this might require special rights / advanced version of the kernel to do so.
- You could try @alejandroliu [PR ](https://github.com/proot-me/PRoot/pull/96) that does copy-on-write, but it applies to all files, not only some selected mounts.
- Way more hard work: add an extension to PRoot, that will create a bind, but also translate each `lstat` and prevent any file opening on write mode.

```shell
proot -r /home/user -b readonly_src/:guest_src/
```
and `guest_src` should be a read-only binding.

I haven't read through the source too carefully yet, but if proot knows who the main process is, maybe it can treat signal terminations of that process differently? I sort of think the whole `last_exit_status` thing should only reflect the main process's exit code, but that may change existing behavior so maybe  would have to sit inside an opt-in flag.

```makefile
KVER = $(shell uname -r)

sed -e 's/^\([0-9][0-9]*\)\.[0-9][0-9]*\.[0-9][0-9]*.*/\1/')
KMIN = $(shell echo $(KVER) | \
sed -e 's/^[0-9][0-9]*\.\([0-9][0-9]*\)\.[0-9][0-9]*.*/\1/')
KREV = $(shell echo $(KVER) | \
sed -e 's/^[0-9][0-9]*\.[0-9][0-9]*\.\([0-9][0-9]*\).*/\1/')

kver_ge = $(shell \
echo test | awk '{if($(KMAJ) < $(1)) {print 0} else { \
if($(KMAJ) > $(1)) {print 1} else { \
if($(KMIN) < $(2)) {print 0} else { \
if($(KMIN) > $(2)) {print 1} else { \
if($(KREV) < $(3)) {print 0} else { print 1 } \
}}}}}' \
)

ifeq ($(call kver_ge,4,8,0),1)
echo great or equal than 4.8.0
else
echo less than 4.8.0
endif

Hi guys. I had sort of similar problem with `ptrace`. In my case, children and sub-children were crashing because of, I think, not checking the result of their `fork()` and something else (a bug, actually). I've found that this problem occurs only with binaries which have subprocesses or multiple threads, so I decided to dig deeper into that. I've found that the tracer was not set by the kernel to the child processes and that, actually, every system call unlisted in my `seccomp` rules was returning `-ENOSYS`, but even when I specified it, others returned ENOSYS and so this lead to a crash. As I did not want to specify all of them and handle all the cases (my debugger really needed to trace only a few system calls), I needed another solution. The solution was to become a tracer of sub-children as well (and actually I also needed that).

I haven't looked much at your code (not at all, actually), but if you have something similar to that, you may look at my problem and solution more detailed on the [stackoverflow](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/56024498/cant-trace-a-subprocesss-syscalls-which-calls-execve-using-ptrace-and-seccomp).
See also: https://github.com/proot-me/proot/issues/106#issuecomment-494680705

Excerpts from an email with libseccomp maintainers.

Per Paul,

> Hi Lucas,
>
> It looks like proot is trying to ptrace another process, possibly
outside it's sandbox, and is running into problems that you are
attributing to seccomp?  Further, it doesn't look like proot itself is
using libseccomp but rather is creating its own seccomp filters.
Without taking a deep dive into proot and its seccomp filters, it is
hard to say what the exact problem may be.  Tracing can be difficult
to get right, especially when seccomp filters are involved.  I'm not
sure if this is your problem, but the issue that comes to mind first
is the "-1" syscall; see the libseccomp documentation around
SCMP_FLTATR_API_TSKIP for more information on that (manpage can be
seen here -> https://github.com/seccomp/libseccomp/blob/master/doc/man/man3/seccomp_attr_set.3).
>
> FWIW, it also appears that you are not handling a lot of ABI specific
details correctly; for example the x32/x86-64 ABI detection needs
special handling as well as the socket/ipc syscalls on platforms which
support both the multiplexed and direct-wired versions.
>
>My guess is it wouldn't be too difficult, maybe Tom has some experience here? As a
bonus, if you adapted proot to use libseccomp, the ABI problems
mentioned above would be taken care of by the library itself, you
wouldn't need to worry about them in proot.

Per Tom,

> I briefly looked through your PRoot code, and while more complex than
the transition I helped work on, at initial glance it doesn't look
too daunting to switch to libseccomp.
>
> Paul brings up several good points of the advantages of using libseccomp
as well.  We (libseccomp) will take care of cBPF creation, ABI issues,
and any syscall changes when a new kernel is released. Maintaining a custom
filter throughout all of that can be challenging.

Per Paul,

>you will just need to ensure that you have added the
required architecture to the filter, look at the seccomp_arch_add(...)
function/manpage for more information.  As long as you add the
architecture before you add the rules, adding a rule to the filter
will add it to the architecture.

>If you want to create different rule sets for different architectures
you can create multiple filters, one for each architecture, and merge
them later using the seccomp_merge(...) function.  There are some
limitations, e.g. same filter attributes, same endianness, etc., but
in general it works just fine.

>In general whilelists tend to be more
restrictive (and potentially "safer" as a result), but they are harder
to maintain.  I believe most general purpose container and sandbox
tools currently use a blacklist approach.

> What's the recommended way to detect a prooted container, as opposed to say, a chrooted container?

I don't think container is the right terminology here.

> I notice that some of your downstream users leave traces to make it obvious (like junest, which exports JUNEST_ENV=1 to children), but I didn't find anything similar in proot itself.

That's a good question!

Here are some questions for you:

- What are the benefits of providing such a feature?
- What are some standard methods used by other projects?
- Would you be willing to submit a PR for us? 😄

I think it should work similar to how `chroot` works now, (See: https://www.freedesktop.org/software/systemd/man/systemd-detect-virt.html#-r).

> I don't think container is the right terminology here.

Heh, I guess "container" as terminology is meaningless anyway, since it could mean just about anything :)

What terminology is more accurate in your eyes? Just "a proot"? I'll make sure we use it as desired in the systemd documentation as well.

> What are the benefits of providing such a feature?

One for me is that I can conditionally do things based on whether I am in proot or not. At its most basic, I might choose to indicate that I am in a different environment in my shell prompt. I may also choose to take some different actions in scripts or programs dependent on that execution environment.

(Lennart goes over some of the design decisions and uses of systemd-detect-virt here, although mostly in the abstract: http://0pointer.de/blog/projects/detect-virt.html)

> What are some standard methods used by other projects?

- For VMs, we usually use the cpuid, or `/proc/device-tree/hypervisor/compatible`. We can also use DMI information and some other tricks.
- For containers, we detect certain container types (eg. OpenVZ) dependent on the environment they provide (for example, `/proc/vz`). For others, we look at /proc/1/sched (which shows non-namespaced pids, but since proot doesn't namespace, this doesn't apply). We also have a few tricks for other cases like WSL.
- For chroot, we look at `/proc/1/root` vs. our root, but this doesn't work for unprivileged users, since `/proc/1/root` is EPERM.

I suspect the most reasonable path to take, if you're amenable, is to emulate a file called `/proc/proot` (or some other path), with what it contains being immaterial. That way we don't pollute the environment of every application, and it has no passive cost.

I'm open to other suggestions as well, though.

I'm completely out of my depth on the low levels of Linux and how `proot` works, but I started looking at the source code, and figured it must be failing on the call to [`ptrace` in `src/tracee/event.c`](https://github.com/proot-me/proot/blob/master/src/tracee/event.c#L77).

I did some googling on `ptrace` and Linux hardening as I suspect Heroku must be locking this down fairly well, and found the following in the [ptrace man pages](http://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/ptrace.2.html) which suggests it may be disabled.

>
> `/proc/sys/kernel/yama/ptrace_scope`
>     On systems with the Yama Linux Security Module (LSM) installed (i.e.,
>     the kernel was configured with CONFIG_SECURITY_YAMA), the
>     /proc/sys/kernel/yama/ptrace_scope file (available since Linux 3.4)
>     can be used to restrict the ability to trace a process with ptrace()
>     (and thus also the ability to use tools such as strace(1) and
>     gdb(1)).  The goal of such restrictions is to prevent attack
>     escalation whereby a compromised process can ptrace-attach to other
>     sensitive processes (e.g., a GPG agent or an SSH session) owned by
>     the user in order to gain additional credentials that may exist in
>     memory and thus expand the scope of the attack.
>
>     More precisely, the Yama LSM limits two types of operations:
>
>     *  Any operation that performs a ptrace access mode
>        PTRACE_MODE_ATTACH check—for example, ptrace() PTRACE_ATTACH.
>        (See the "Ptrace access mode checking" discussion above.)
>
>     *  ptrace() PTRACE_TRACEME.
> 

I ran `cat /proc/sys/kernel/yama/ptrace_scope` during slug compilation and got a value of `1`, so I guess this explains why I get the permission denied error.

Further reading revealed the process needs `CAP_SYS_PTRACE` capability and I there isn't a way to do this on Heroku I suspect.

Proot is a wrapper, and thus much closer to a shell. The important thing would be to reproduce transparently the WIFSIGNALED, WTERMSIG, WIFEXITED, WEXITSTATUS of the child process.

This can be accomplished by checking whether the child exited normally (and if so exit with the same status) or was killed by a signal (and if so kill the proot process with the same signal).

Failing that, the 128 - SIGNAL convention is quite widespread (shells, perl) and allows whoever calls proot to figure out what the wrapped command did.

If you lose the normal-exit / signaled status of the child process and the signal number (if any), the only option for me is to 
- wrap the child process in a wrapper that saves WIFSIGNALED, WTERMSIG, WIFEXITED, WEXITSTATUS to a temporary file
- call that wrapper from proot, then
- parse the temporary file in yet *another* wrapper.

Which makes little sense, since proot should be a transparent wrapper itself.

> Since Linux 2.6.39, `pathname` can be an empty string, in which case the call operates on the symbolic link referred to by `dirfd` (which should have been obtained using open(2) with the `O_PATH` and `O_NOFOLLOW` flags).

proot doesn't handle this case, and I'm not sure if simply making `detranslate_path` ignore an empty `t_referrer` is correct. In fact, I'm not sure if proot's readlinkat handling is otherwise correct at all.

One specific problem I encountered when trying to make apt work under proot:

A process running under `proot -0` sees files owned by the unprivileged user running proot as owned by root. However it does not do similar mapping for other system users or groups.

For example, apt likes to have `/var/lib/apt/lists/partial` owned by system user `_apt`. This then leads to various `permission denied` errors, because the unprivileged user running proot does not have permission to work with files owned by `_apt`.

I could not find any official documentation explicitly stating this, but the function signature documented on the manpage as well as in the [official GLIBC documentation](https://www.gnu.org/software/libc/manual/html_node/Executing-a-File.html) implies `argc` to be greater than, or equal to 1, which is also mirrored by the [current GLIBC implementation](https://github.com/bminor/glibc/blob/master/posix/execlp.c).

Because of this the condition for `argc == 0` never holds and the test results in an infinite loop.

I think my fix is unproblematic, because the test was added to assert that proot does not crash when `execlp` is called with the `NULL` pointer for `arg` and `argc` being 0 was just a convenient way to distinguish the parent and child processes.

```console

root@machine:~#
```

- The postinstall script of another core Ubuntu package `dmsetup`. Quite a lot of packages depend on this too.

I *think* I know what the problem is: The readlinkat(2) manpage states:

> Since  Linux 2.6.39, pathname can be an empty string, in which case the call operates on the symbolic link referred to by dirfd

This case appears not to be supported by proot when I read the source correctly.
